block.title: Opening a glibc proof from a cold checkout
block.p: The transliteration proof used to load Intel cache discovery and getopt’s option table to describe memory in Hello’s image. Giving the object layouts and the packing of literal bytes their own modules reduced its transitive glibc imports from 737 to 436.

On swa, rq open libio/LibioWConvTranslit.v --theorem flags_step reached the first goal in 382 seconds with the old imports and 124 seconds with the new ones. Both runs started with an empty interface directory, the same compiled Nanofil model and eight make jobs. Other builds shared the host. The worker’s peak memory fell from 3.0 GiB to 0.6 GiB. Reloading the new session took 0.43 seconds and reused eighteen sentences.

The Intel descriptor checker exports twelve specifications. Each preserves the abstract bounds on the caller’s objects and returns a machine word. Rocq checks that invariant discovery produces precisely those specifications and that each plan passes the verifier. Compiling the interface with rocq c -vos against the same full dependency objects took 163.4 seconds before the change and 1.65 seconds after it.

For comparison, a clean full proof build on swa at revision 4dfe8757cdcb compiled all 1,440 glibc sources against the pinned Nanofil model. With twelve jobs, build.sh took 17 minutes 26 seconds. The sampled sum of resident memory across its processes peaked at 30.7 GiB. This measures ordinary full Rocq compilation with a prebuilt model. At that revision, the push and scheduled checks also ran probes and assumption audits.
